title: Ang 1349–1350: Kabir in Prabhati
hook: first came the light; don't call the scriptures false
tomorrow: a man covered in holy marks, with a knife in his heart. who is he?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the third, fourth and fifth Gurus sang at dawn in Prabhati. Dawn hymns. Now the dawn raga turns to the Bhagats, and Kabir goes first.

Third period, and the argument is already going. Somebody in the back says every holy book is made up. Somebody else says only theirs isn't. Phones out, voices up, the teacher tapping the board for quiet. Kabir's hymn on ang 1349 speaks into a room like that: people sure the other side's books were false. He doesn't pick a side. He starts somewhere older than every book in the room.
screen: `EVERY HOLY BOOK IS MADE UP.` → `ONLY OURS ISN'T.` → `KABIR STARTS EARLIER.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the hymn opens: first God made the light, and all people are of God's making. From one light the whole world welled up. So who is good, and who is bad? Notice the order. Before anyone's scripture, before anyone's label, there is light. Kabir calls God Allah here, and the light noor, words from the Muslim world, and he aims them at everyone listening. Then he turns to clay. One clay, shaped many ways by one Maker; there's no fault in the clay pots, and no fault in the Potter. Then, on the next page, in another hymn, the line that answers the classroom. In paraphrase: don't call the Vedas and the other scriptures false. False is the one who doesn't reflect. It's a careful line. Kabir doesn't say every book says the same thing. He doesn't say books don't matter. He moves the word false off the page and onto the reader: the one who reads without looking inward. So the hymn's question comes back around. Who's good, and who's bad? Kabir's answer is to look at where everyone came from. First, the light.
screen: `FROM ONE LIGHT, THE WHOLE WORLD.` · `ONE CLAY, MANY POTS.` · `DON'T CALL THE SCRIPTURES FALSE.` · `FALSE IS WHOEVER WON'T REFLECT.` · then, large: `FIRST, THE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Say the hymn's question out loud, slowly: from one light, who is good and who is bad? Then let the quiet hold it. If a face comes to mind, someone you've filed under bad, set it beside the word light and leave it there.
Ang 1349. Where Kabir, in the dawn raga, starts with the light, before anyone's book or label.
Hold onto this: first, the light, before anyone argued about whose book is true. See you at dawn.

screen: `DAY 1611 COUNTS.` → `A WALK THROUGH THE GRANTH · 165 OF 180.` → `TOMORROW: A MAN IN HOLY MARKS, A KNIFE INSIDE. WHO?`

howItsDone: Kabir's hymn 'from one light the whole world welled up' is sung in Prabhati, the dawn raga, and quoted in Sikh talks and kirtan on the oneness of people.

fork.setup: one friend calls her grandmother's prayer book 'superstition.' another says only his own book is true. you get one sentence. what does Kabir's hymn give you?
options: start where everyone came from, one light; then ask who actually reflects on what they read.
tell them Kabir proved every religion is really one and the same religion.
stay out of it; Kabir says books don't matter, only the light inside does.
fork.reveal: the hymn starts at the light, then moves 'false' off the book and onto the reader who won't reflect. it never says all the same, and never says books don't matter.

original.note: Gurmukhi: ek noor, one light, from Kabir's hymn on ang 1349.

trapdoor: what you thought: a poet saying all religions are one.
what it means: Kabir starts before every book and label, with one light, and calls false the reader who won't reflect, not the scripture.
what a scholar hears: the hymn speaks in Muslim words, Allah and noor, to Hindu and Muslim listeners alike; kateb is the Bhagats' word for the scriptures beside the Vedas.
guess: where Kabir says all people come from one light
where Guru Nanak opens the dawn raga Prabhati
where Farid's couplets begin in the Granth
recall: Prabhati opens: Guru Nanak at dawn

chat.says: kid in lit class said all holy books are fake. my college essay roasts him. good idea?
options: Kabir won't call anyone's scripture false; false is whoever won't reflect. write about reflecting, not roasting.
roast away: Kabir says the books are all false, and only the light inside you is real.
skip it: Kabir says every holy book teaches exactly the same thing, so there's nothing to argue.
chat.meaning: Kabir: don't call the Vedas and the other scriptures false; false is the one who doesn't reflect. He starts with one light, not a winner.

Kabir.meaning: a Bhagat, a poet-saint whose hymns the Gurus kept

Prabhati.meaning: the dawn raga, near the end of the Granth

noor.meaning: light, a word from Arabic and Persian

Allah.meaning: God, in Arabic; Kabir uses the name here

sources.ref: Ang 1349 (Prabhati, Bhagat Kabir: avval allah noor upaaiaa, kudrat ke sabh bande; ek noor te sabh jag upjiaa, kaun bhale ko mande; and the clay and the Potter), paraphrased
Ang 1350 (Prabhati, Bhagat Kabir: bed kateb kahahu mat jhoothe, jhoothaa jo na bichaarai), paraphrased

notes: 2026-10-15 v3 written: shape story (a classroom argument about whose books are 'fake'; Kabir's hymn starts before every book, with one light). Unity: the hymn's own oneness of people, with the careful line that it never says 'all the same'.

Confirm the paraphrases at ang 1349 (avval allah noor upaaiaa...; maatee ek anek bhaant kar saajee saajanhaarai) and ang 1350 (bed kateb kahahu mat jhoothe, jhoothaa jo na bichaarai), and that the second line is in the following Prabhati hymn of Kabir.
The 'bed kateb' hymn goes on to question a mullah's practice; the lesson leaves that part out on purpose to keep no tradition as a foil. Please confirm that's fair.
Trapdoor: 'kateb' read as the scriptures of the Semitic traditions (Torah, Psalms, Gospel, Qur'an) is the standard gloss; kept general on purpose.
